about: Microeconomics 1 (BUSI40006) is listed in the 2024-25 programme specification as a compulsory 7.5 ECTS module in Year 1 of Imperial Business School's BSc Economics, Finance and Data Science, taught in the Spring term after the Autumn-term core modules Mathematical Foundations and Probability and Statistics. It introduces how individuals and firms make decisions and interact in markets. Imperial does not publish a topic list or module description for it, so the topics here follow the standard first-year microeconomics syllabus; check them against your lecture schedule. The programme specification says assessment across the programme mixes coursework (such as problem sets) with unseen examinations, but it does not give a breakdown for this module.

notes.h: Supply, demand, elasticity and tax incidence
notes.body:
Most introductory microeconomics courses begin with the competitive market model, and it is the reference point for everything that follows. On a programme with a strong maths core like this one, expect to solve these models algebraically, not just with diagrams.

Demand and supply
- The demand curve Qd(P) shows how much buyers want at each price, holding income, other prices and tastes fixed. It normally slopes down (the law of demand).
- The supply curve Qs(P) shows how much sellers offer at each price, holding input prices and technology fixed. It normally slopes up.
- A change in the good's own price moves along a curve; a change in anything else (income, prices of substitutes or complements, input costs) shifts the curve.
- Equilibrium is the price at which Qd(P) = Qs(P). At any higher price there is excess supply; at any lower price, excess demand.

Worked example
- Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 3P − 20. Setting them equal: 100 − 2P = 3P − 20, so P* = 24 and Q* = 52.
- Comparative statics: if demand shifts out, both P* and Q* rise; if supply shifts out, P* falls and Q* rises.

Elasticities
- Own-price elasticity of demand: ε = (dQ/dP)(P/Q), the percentage change in quantity for a 1% change in price. It is negative for normal downward-sloping demand.
- In the example at equilibrium, ε = −2 × 24/52 ≈ −0.92: demand is inelastic (|ε| < 1). Supply elasticity there is 3 × 24/52 ≈ 1.38.
- Elastic (|ε| > 1): a price cut raises total revenue. Inelastic (|ε| < 1): a price cut lowers revenue. Unit elastic: revenue unchanged. This follows from d(PQ)/dP = Q(1 + ε).
- Along a straight-line demand curve, elasticity changes: elastic at high prices, inelastic at low prices.
- Income elasticity (dQ/dm)(m/Q): positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods. Cross-price elasticity: positive for substitutes, negative for complements.
- Determinants of price elasticity: availability of substitutes, share of the budget, time horizon (more elastic in the long run), and how broadly the market is defined.

Surplus
- Consumer surplus (CS) is the area under the demand curve and above the price; producer surplus (PS) is the area above the supply curve and below the price.
- In the example, demand hits zero at P = 50 and supply at P = 20/3, so CS = ½ × (50 − 24) × 52 = 676 and PS = ½ × (24 − 20/3) × 52 ≈ 450.7.

Tax incidence
- A per-unit tax t drives a wedge between the price buyers pay (Pb) and the price sellers keep (Ps = Pb − t).
- With t = 5 on sellers in the example, supply becomes Qs = 3(Pb − 5) − 20. Solving 100 − 2Pb = 3Pb − 35 gives Pb = 27, Ps = 22, Q = 46.
- Buyers bear 3 of the 5 and sellers 2. The side of the market that is less elastic bears more of the tax, whoever legally pays it.
- Tax revenue = 5 × 46 = 230; deadweight loss = ½ × 5 × (52 − 46) = 15.
- Price ceilings below equilibrium cause shortages; price floors above it cause surpluses.

Exam tips: always state which variable is held constant when you draw a curve, show the elasticity calculation at a specific point, and in tax questions report Pb, Ps, quantity, revenue and deadweight loss.

notes.h: Consumer preferences, utility and indifference curves
notes.body:
Consumer theory starts from what people prefer, not from utility as a measurable quantity. Utility is a convenient way to represent preferences.

Preferences and their axioms
- The consumer compares bundles (x, y). x ≽ y means "x is at least as good as y".
- Completeness: for any two bundles, the consumer can rank them (x ≽ y or y ≽ x or both).
- Transitivity: if x ≽ y and y ≽ z then x ≽ z. Without it, choices could cycle.
- Monotonicity ("more is better"): more of every good is strictly preferred. This makes indifference curves slope downwards and makes higher curves better.
- Convexity: averages are at least as good as extremes. This makes indifference curves bowed towards the origin (diminishing MRS).
- Continuity: small changes in bundles cause small changes in preference, which allows a continuous utility function.

Utility functions
- u(x, y) represents preferences if u(A) ≥ u(B) exactly when A ≽ B.
- Utility is ordinal: only the ranking matters. Any strictly increasing transformation (for example ln u, u², 3u + 7 when u > 0) represents the same preferences, and gives the same indifference curves and choices.
- Marginal utility MUx = ∂u/∂x. Its size is not meaningful on its own, because a transformation changes it, but ratios of marginal utilities are meaningful.

Indifference curves and the marginal rate of substitution
- An indifference curve joins all bundles with the same utility. Two indifference curves cannot cross if preferences are monotonic and transitive.
- The marginal rate of substitution MRS = MUx / MUy is the rate at which the consumer is willing to give up y for one more unit of x. It equals minus the slope of the indifference curve, dy/dx = −MUx/MUy.
- Diminishing MRS: as the consumer has more x, they will give up less y for an extra unit of it. This is equivalent to convex indifference curves.
- Example: u = xy². MUx = y², MUy = 2xy, so MRS = y/(2x). At (4, 2), MRS = 0.25.

Standard utility functions (learn their shapes)
- Cobb–Douglas: u = x^a y^(1−a), 0 < a < 1. MRS = [a/(1 − a)](y/x). Smooth convex indifference curves.
- Perfect substitutes: u = ax + by. Straight-line indifference curves with constant MRS = a/b.
- Perfect complements: u = min(ax, by). L-shaped indifference curves with corners on the line ax = by; MRS undefined at the corner.
- Quasilinear: u = v(x) + y. MRS = v′(x) depends only on x, so indifference curves are vertical shifts of each other and demand for x does not depend on income (at interior solutions).

Why it matters
- These axioms let us derive demand curves from individual optimisation, rather than assuming them. The rest of the course (and later data science applications such as demand estimation) builds on this.

Exam tips: always compute MRS as a ratio of marginal utilities, check whether a proposed function is a monotonic transformation of another, and sketch the indifference map for each standard functional form.

notes.h: Budget constraints and optimal consumer choice
notes.body:
Consumers choose the best bundle they can afford. Putting the budget constraint together with preferences gives demand functions.

The budget constraint
- With prices px, py and income m: px x + py y ≤ m. With monotonic preferences, all income is spent, so the constraint holds with equality.
- The budget line has intercepts m/px and m/py and slope −px/py (the market rate at which y can be traded for x).
- Income up: parallel outward shift. A rise in px: the line pivots inwards around the y-intercept.
- Multiplying all prices and income by the same factor leaves the budget set unchanged, so demand is homogeneous of degree zero in (px, py, m): there is no money illusion.

The optimum: tangency
- With smooth, convex preferences and an interior solution, the best bundle is where the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line: MRS = px/py.
- Equivalently MUx/px = MUy/py: the last pound spent on each good gives the same extra utility.
- If MUx/px > MUy/py, switching spending from y to x raises utility, so the consumer is not yet at the optimum.

The Lagrangian method
- Maximise u(x, y) subject to px x + py y = m. Form L = u(x, y) + λ(m − px x − py y).
- First-order conditions: ∂u/∂x = λpx, ∂u/∂y = λpy, and the constraint. Dividing the first two gives MRS = px/py.
- The multiplier λ is the marginal utility of income: how much the maximum utility rises per extra pound.

Cobb–Douglas demands
- For u = x^a y^(1−a): x* = a m/px and y* = (1 − a) m/py. The consumer spends a fixed share a of income on x.
- Example: u = x^½ y^½, m = 100, px = 2, py = 5. Then x* = 0.5 × 100/2 = 25 and y* = 0.5 × 100/5 = 10. Check: 2 × 25 + 5 × 10 = 100.
- Taking logs first (ln u = a ln x + (1 − a) ln y) often makes the algebra easier, and gives the same answer because utility is ordinal.

Corner and kinked solutions
- Perfect substitutes u = ax + by: compare a/px with b/py and spend everything on the good with the higher marginal utility per pound. If equal, any bundle on the budget line is optimal. Tangency fails here.
- Perfect complements u = min(x, y): the consumer buys at the corner x = y, so x = y = m/(px + py). The MRS condition does not apply at a kink.
- Quasilinear preferences can also give a corner where the consumer buys none of one good.

Indirect utility
- Substituting demands back into u gives the indirect utility function V(px, py, m): the highest utility achievable at those prices and income. It rises with m and falls with each price. For Cobb–Douglas, V = (a/px)^a ((1 − a)/py)^(1−a) m.

Exam tips: state and check the second-order (convexity) assumptions before using tangency, always verify the bundle exhausts the budget, and look for corner solutions whenever utility is linear or has a kink.

When a price changes, two things happen at once: the good becomes relatively cheaper or dearer (substitution effect), and the consumer's purchasing power changes (income effect). Separating them explains the shape of demand curves.

Normal, inferior and Giffen goods
- Normal good: demand rises with income. Inferior good: demand falls with income.
- The Engel curve plots quantity demanded against income at fixed prices.
- Giffen good: demand rises when its own price rises. This needs the good to be inferior and the income effect to outweigh the substitution effect. Giffen goods are very rare in practice.

The substitution effect
- It is the change in demand when relative prices change but the consumer is compensated so that their "real income" is held constant.
- For a price fall, the substitution effect never reduces demand for the good (it never moves quantity in the same direction as the price). This holds for every good with convex preferences; with smooth, strictly convex preferences it strictly increases demand, while in special cases such as perfect complements it is zero.

Two ways to compensate
- Slutsky compensation: adjust income so the consumer can just afford the original bundle at the new prices. Required income m′ = m + x₀(p₁ − p₀).
- Hicks compensation: adjust income so the consumer can just reach the original utility level at the new prices. This uses the Hicksian (compensated) demand h(p, u), which comes from minimising expenditure for a target utility.
- For small price changes the two give almost the same answer (they coincide in the limit of an infinitesimal change); for large changes they differ noticeably.

Worked example
- u = xy (Cobb–Douglas with a = ½), m = 120, py = 1, and px falls from 3 to 2. Demand is x = m/(2px).
- Original x₀ = 120/6 = 20 (and y = 60). New x₁ = 120/4 = 30. Total effect = +10.
- Slutsky: m′ = 120 + 20 × (2 − 3) = 100. At the new prices with income 100, x = 100/4 = 25. Substitution effect = 25 − 20 = 5; income effect = 30 − 25 = 5.
- Hicks: original utility is 20 × 60 = 1200. Minimising cost at px = 2, py = 1 subject to xy = 1200 gives y = 2x, so x = √600 ≈ 24.49. Substitution effect ≈ 4.49; income effect ≈ 5.51.
- Both decompositions show that x is a normal good here: the income effect reinforces the substitution effect.

The Slutsky equation
- In calculus form: ∂x/∂px = ∂h/∂px − x ∂x/∂m.
- The first term is the (Hicksian) substitution effect and is never positive. The second is the income effect.
- For a normal good (∂x/∂m > 0) both terms are negative, so demand definitely slopes down. For an inferior good the income effect works the other way; only if it is large enough is the good Giffen.

Duality and welfare (useful extras)
- The expenditure function e(p, u) gives the minimum cost of reaching utility u; for u = xy it is e = 2√(px py u).
- Compensating variation (CV): the change in income needed after a price change to bring the consumer back to their original utility level. In the example CV = 120 − e(2, 1, 1200) = 120 − 2√2400 ≈ 22.02.

Exam tips: draw the three bundles (original, compensated, final) on one diagram, label which movement is which effect, and say whether you are using Slutsky or Hicks compensation.

The theory of the firm mirrors consumer theory: production functions play the role of utility, isoquants replace indifference curves, and cost minimisation replaces utility maximisation.

Production functions
- Q = f(K, L) gives the maximum output from capital K and labour L.
- Marginal product of labour MPL = ∂f/∂L. The law of diminishing marginal returns says MPL eventually falls as L rises with K held fixed.
- The short run is a period in which at least one input (usually K) is fixed; in the long run all inputs are variable.
- An isoquant shows all (K, L) combinations giving the same output. Its slope is −MRTS, where MRTS = MPL/MPK, the rate at which labour can replace capital while keeping output constant.

Returns to scale
- Compare f(tK, tL) with t f(K, L) for t > 1: increasing returns if larger, constant if equal, decreasing if smaller.
- For Cobb–Douglas Q = A K^α L^β, returns to scale are increasing, constant or decreasing as α + β is greater than, equal to or less than 1.
- Returns to scale (all inputs scaled) are a different idea from diminishing marginal returns (one input varied).

Cost minimisation
- Choose K and L to minimise wL + rK subject to f(K, L) = Q. At an interior solution the isoquant is tangent to an isocost line: MRTS = MPL/MPK = w/r, or MPL/w = MPK/r.
- Example: Q = K^½ L^½, w = 4, r = 1. MPL/MPK = K/L = 4, so K = 4L. Then Q = √(4L²) = 2L, so L = Q/2 and K = 2Q. Total cost C(Q) = 4(Q/2) + 2Q = 4Q. Average and marginal cost are both 4: constant returns to scale give constant long-run average cost.

Cost concepts
- Economic cost includes opportunity cost, not just accounting cost. Sunk costs cannot be recovered and should not affect forward-looking decisions.
- Total cost TC = fixed cost FC + variable cost VC. Average total cost ATC = TC/Q, average variable cost AVC = VC/Q, average fixed cost AFC = FC/Q.
- Marginal cost MC = dTC/dQ. MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minimum points, because an average falls while the marginal is below it and rises while the marginal is above it.

Short run versus long run
- With K fixed at 16 in the example, Q = 4√L, so L = Q²/16 and short-run cost is STC = 16 + Q²/4 (fixed cost 16 from capital).
- SMC = Q/2 and SAC = 16/Q + Q/4. SAC is minimised where SAC = SMC: 16/Q = Q/4, so Q = 8 and SAC = 4.
- This equals the long-run average cost of 4, and K = 16 is exactly the long-run optimal capital for Q = 8 (K = 2Q). The long-run average cost curve is the lower envelope of the short-run curves.
- Economies of scale: long-run average cost falls as output rises (linked to increasing returns to scale, but also to input prices and specialisation).

Exam tips: always check the sign of each partial derivative, quote the tangency condition before solving, and draw MC passing through the minima of AVC and ATC.

notes.h: Perfect competition, supply and economic welfare
notes.body:
Perfect competition is the benchmark market structure. It shows how independent profit-maximising firms can produce an efficient outcome, and it is the standard against which monopoly and market failures are judged.

Assumptions
- Many buyers and sellers, each too small to affect price (price takers).
- A homogeneous product.
- Perfect information.
- Free entry and exit in the long run.

The firm's short-run decision
- Profit π = Pq − C(q). The price-taking firm chooses q where P = MC, on the rising part of the MC curve.
- Shutdown rule: produce only if P ≥ minimum AVC. If P is below it, revenue does not cover the costs the firm could avoid by producing nothing, so it shuts down and loses only its fixed (sunk) costs.
- A firm can produce at a loss in the short run, as long as price covers average variable cost.
- So the firm's short-run supply curve is its MC curve above minimum AVC. The market supply curve is the horizontal sum of firms' supply curves.

The long run
- Positive profits attract entry, which shifts market supply out and lowers price; losses cause exit.
- Long-run equilibrium (identical firms): P = MC = minimum long-run average cost, with zero economic profit (firms still earn a normal return, which is counted as a cost).
- With identical firms and constant input prices, the long-run market supply curve is horizontal at minimum LRAC.

Worked example
- Each firm has C(q) = 100 + q², so MC = 2q and AC = 100/q + q. Market demand is Q = 1000 − 10P.
- Minimum AC: 100/q = q gives q = 10 and AC = 20. So the long-run price is 20, each firm makes 10, market output is 1000 − 200 = 800, and there are 800/10 = 80 firms.
- Suppose there are 100 firms in the short run (with the 100 treated as sunk). Each supplies q = P/2, so market supply is 50P. Then 1000 − 10P = 50P gives P = 50/3 ≈ 16.67 and q = 25/3 ≈ 8.33. Profit = Pq − 100 − q² = 625/9 − 100 ≈ −30.6. Firms stay open (P > minimum AVC = 0) but make losses, so some exit in the long run until P returns to 20.

Welfare
- Total surplus = consumer surplus + producer surplus. In competitive equilibrium, every trade with willingness to pay above marginal cost happens, and no other trade does, so total surplus is maximised.
- This is an informal version of the First Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics: under conditions including no externalities, complete markets and price-taking, a competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient (nobody can be made better off without someone being made worse off).
- Efficiency is not fairness: a Pareto-efficient outcome can be very unequal.
- Interventions such as taxes, price ceilings and price floors cause deadweight losses by blocking mutually beneficial trades.

Exam tips: distinguish clearly between the shutdown condition (P vs min AVC) and the exit condition (P vs min AC); show both firm-level and market-level diagrams; and always state that long-run profit is zero in economic, not accounting, terms.

A monopolist is the single seller in a market with barriers to entry. Unlike a competitive firm, it faces the whole downward-sloping market demand curve, so selling more means lowering the price.

Sources of monopoly power
- Legal barriers: patents, licences, franchises.
- Control of a key input.
- Economies of scale so large that one firm can supply the market most cheaply (natural monopoly).
- Network effects and strategic behaviour by incumbents.

Marginal revenue
- With inverse demand P(Q), revenue is R = P(Q)Q and marginal revenue MR = P + Q dP/dQ, which is less than P.
- In elasticity form: MR = P(1 + 1/ε). So MR > 0 only where demand is elastic (|ε| > 1). A monopolist with positive marginal cost always produces on the elastic part of demand.
- For linear demand P = a − bQ, MR = a − 2bQ: same intercept, twice the slope.

The monopoly optimum
- Choose Q where MR = MC, then charge the price on the demand curve at that quantity.
- Mark-up rule: (P − MC)/P = −1/ε = 1/|ε|. The left-hand side is the Lerner index of market power. The less elastic the demand, the bigger the mark-up.
- A monopolist has no supply curve: the quantity it sells at a given price depends on the shape of demand, not only on cost.

Worked example
- P = 100 − 2Q and MC = 20 (constant, no fixed cost).
- MR = 100 − 4Q = 20 gives Q = 20 and P = 60. Profit = (60 − 20) × 20 = 800.
- Under competition P = MC = 20 and Q = 40.
- Deadweight loss = ½ × (60 − 20) × (40 − 20) = 400. Consumer surplus under monopoly = ½ × (100 − 60) × 20 = 400.
- Check: elasticity at Q = 20 is (dQ/dP)(P/Q) = (−½)(60/20) = −1.5, and the Lerner index (60 − 20)/60 = 2/3 = 1/1.5.

Price discrimination
- First degree (perfect): charge each buyer their willingness to pay. Output is efficient (no deadweight loss) but the firm captures all the surplus.
- Second degree: offer a menu (quantity discounts, versions) and let buyers self-select.
- Third degree: charge different prices to identifiable groups (students, regions). Set MR₁ = MR₂ = MC; the group with less elastic demand pays more.
- Example: P₁ = 100 − Q₁, P₂ = 60 − Q₂, MC = 20. Market 1: 100 − 2Q₁ = 20 gives Q₁ = 40, P₁ = 60. Market 2: 60 − 2Q₂ = 20 gives Q₂ = 20, P₂ = 40. Elasticities at these points are −1.5 and −2, so the less elastic market pays the higher price. Profit = 40 × 40 + 20 × 20 = 2000.
- Discrimination needs market power, a way to identify groups, and no resale between them.

Policy
- Remedies include competition law, breaking up firms, and regulation. For natural monopolies, marginal-cost pricing can leave the firm with losses (because average cost exceeds marginal cost), so regulators often use average-cost pricing or price caps.

Exam tips: derive MR before setting it equal to MC, read price off the demand curve (not the MR curve), and quote the Lerner index to link mark-ups to elasticity.

When a few firms dominate a market, each firm's best choice depends on what the others do. Game theory provides the tools to analyse this strategic interaction.

Games in normal form
- A game lists the players, their strategies and their payoffs for every combination of strategies.
- A strictly dominant strategy is best whatever the other players do.
- A Nash equilibrium (after John Nash, 1950) is a strategy profile in which each player's strategy is a best response to the others: no one can gain by deviating alone.
- Finding pure-strategy equilibria: for each column, mark the row player's best payoff; for each row, mark the column player's best payoff; cells with both marked are Nash equilibria.

The prisoner's dilemma
- Example payoffs (row, column): (Cooperate, Cooperate) = (3, 3), (Cooperate, Defect) = (0, 5), (Defect, Cooperate) = (5, 0), (Defect, Defect) = (1, 1).
- Defect is strictly dominant for both, so (Defect, Defect) is the unique Nash equilibrium, even though both would be better off cooperating. Individual and collective interest diverge.
- This explains why cartels are unstable and why repeated interaction can matter.

Mixed strategies
- A player may randomise. In a mixed-strategy equilibrium each player mixes so that the opponent is indifferent between the strategies the opponent uses.
- Example: payoffs (U, L) = (4, 3), (U, R) = (1, 1), (D, L) = (2, 0), (D, R) = (3, 2). There are two pure equilibria, (U, L) and (D, R). There is also a mixed equilibrium where each player puts probability ½ on each strategy: if row plays U with probability p, column is indifferent when 3p = p + 2(1 − p), so p = ½; if column plays L with probability q, row is indifferent when 4q + (1 − q) = 2q + 3(1 − q), so q = ½.

Sequential games
- Represented as game trees and solved by backward induction. The result is a subgame perfect equilibrium, which rules out non-credible threats.

Oligopoly models (inverse demand P = a − bQ, marginal cost c)
- Cournot (1838): firms choose quantities simultaneously. Firm 1 maximises (a − b(q₁ + q₂) − c)q₁, giving best response q₁ = (a − c − bq₂)/(2b). The symmetric Nash equilibrium is q = (a − c)/(3b) for each firm.
- Example: a = 120, b = 1, c = 30. Each firm produces 30, total 60, price 60, profit 900 each.
- Comparison: monopoly produces 45 at price 75 (profit 2025); perfect competition produces 90 at price 30. Cournot lies in between.
- Collusion: if the two split the monopoly output (22.5 each), each earns 1012.5, but each would gain by deviating to its best response 33.75, earning about 1139. This is the prisoner's dilemma in quantities.
- Bertrand (1883): firms choose prices for an identical product. With equal constant marginal cost, the unique equilibrium is P = MC, even with only two firms (the Bertrand paradox). Product differentiation or capacity limits soften this.
- Stackelberg (1934): a leader chooses quantity first, knowing the follower's best response. In the example the leader produces 45, the follower 22.5, and price is 52.5. The leader earns more than under Cournot (1012.5 versus 900): commitment is valuable.

Exam tips: always write out best-response functions before solving; check equilibria by confirming no player can gain by a unilateral deviation; and compare quantities, prices and profits across models in a small table.

notes.h: Market failure: externalities and public goods
notes.body:
Competitive markets are efficient only under certain conditions. When those conditions fail, the market outcome is inefficient and there may be a case for intervention.

Externalities
- An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on people outside a transaction and is not reflected in the price.
- Negative externality (for example pollution): marginal social cost MSC = marginal private cost MPC + marginal external cost MEC. The market produces where demand meets MPC, so it overproduces relative to the social optimum where demand meets MSC.
- Positive externality (for example vaccination or research): marginal social benefit exceeds private benefit, so the market underproduces.

Worked example
- Demand (marginal benefit) P = 100 − Q, private marginal cost MPC = 20 + Q, and a constant external cost of 10 per unit.
- Market: 100 − Q = 20 + Q gives Q = 40 and P = 60.
- Social optimum: 100 − Q = 30 + Q gives Q = 35 and P = 65.
- Deadweight loss = ½ × 10 × (40 − 35) = 25: the units from 35 to 40 cost society more than they are worth.

Remedies
- Pigouvian tax (after A. C. Pigou, The Economics of Welfare, 1920): a per-unit tax equal to the marginal external cost at the optimum. Here a tax of 10 moves private cost onto MSC and the market chooses Q = 35. A Pigouvian subsidy works the other way for positive externalities.
- Quantity regulation: caps or standards. Simple, but they need the regulator to know the efficient level and do not minimise abatement costs across firms.
- Tradable permits (cap and trade): fix total emissions and let firms trade permits, so abatement happens where it is cheapest.
- The Coase theorem (Ronald Coase, "The Problem of Social Cost", 1960): if property rights are well defined and transaction costs are low, private bargaining reaches the efficient outcome whoever holds the rights. The allocation of rights affects who pays, not the efficient quantity. In practice, transaction costs and many affected parties often make bargaining impossible.

Classifying goods
- Rival: one person's use reduces what is available to others. Excludable: people can be prevented from using it.
- Private goods: rival and excludable (food).
- Public goods: non-rival and non-excludable (national defence, street lighting).
- Common resources: rival but non-excludable (fish stocks). They are prone to overuse, the "tragedy of the commons" (Garrett Hardin, 1968).
- Club goods: excludable but non-rival up to capacity (subscription streaming, a private park).

Public goods
- Because no one can be excluded, each person has an incentive to free ride on others' contributions, so private markets under-provide public goods.
- Efficient provision (the Samuelson condition, 1954): provide the good up to the point where the sum of all individuals' marginal benefits (MRS) equals marginal cost. Because the good is non-rival, we add marginal benefits vertically, not quantities horizontally.
- Governments often provide public goods through taxation, but they face their own information problem: people have little incentive to reveal their true valuations.

Other sources of market failure (often previewed in a first course)
- Market power (see monopoly).
- Asymmetric information, as in George Akerlof's "market for lemons" (1970), where poorly informed buyers can drive good-quality products out of the market.

Exam tips: draw MPC and MSC on the same diagram, shade the deadweight loss triangle, and state the conditions for the Coase theorem before applying it.

cards.b: ε = (dQ/dP) × (P/Q): the percentage change in quantity demanded per 1% change in price.
d(PQ)/dP = Q(1 + ε). If |ε| > 1 a price cut raises revenue; if |ε| < 1 it lowers revenue; if |ε| = 1 revenue is unchanged.

cards.f: Movement along vs shift of a demand curve
cards.b: A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; a change in income, other prices or tastes shifts the whole curve.
The less elastic side of the market bears more of it, regardless of whether buyers or sellers legally pay.
The area under the demand curve and above the market price, up to the quantity traded: buyers' willingness to pay minus what they pay.
Positive for substitutes (price of one up, demand for the other up); negative for complements.

cards.f: Deadweight loss of a per-unit tax t (linear curves)
cards.b: ½ × t × (fall in quantity traded): the surplus lost on trades that no longer happen.
Any two bundles can be compared: either x ≽ y, or y ≽ x, or both.
If x ≽ y and y ≽ z, then x ≽ z. It rules out preference cycles.
Only the ranking of bundles matters; any strictly increasing transformation of u represents the same preferences.
MRS = MUx/MUy: the amount of y the consumer will give up for one more unit of x; minus the slope of the indifference curve.

cards.f: MRS for Cobb–Douglas u = x^a y^(1−a)
Perfect complements: utility and indifference curves
cards.b: u = min(ax, by); L-shaped indifference curves with corners on the ray ax = by.
u = ax + by; straight-line indifference curves with constant MRS = a/b.

cards.f: What property gives convex indifference curves?
cards.b: Convex preferences (averages preferred to extremes), equivalent to a diminishing MRS.

cards.f: Slope of the budget line px x + py y = m
cards.b: −px/py (with x on the horizontal axis).

cards.f: Tangency condition for an interior optimum
cards.b: MRS = px/py, equivalently MUx/px = MUy/py.

cards.f: Cobb–Douglas demands for u = x^a y^(1−a)
cards.b: x* = a m/px and y* = (1 − a) m/py: constant budget shares a and 1 − a.

cards.f: Meaning of the Lagrange multiplier λ in consumer choice
cards.b: The marginal utility of income: the rise in maximised utility per extra unit of income.

cards.f: Homogeneity of degree zero of demand
cards.b: Scaling all prices and income by the same factor leaves demand unchanged (no money illusion).

cards.f: Optimal choice with perfect substitutes u = ax + by
cards.b: Corner solution: spend all income on x if a/px > b/py, on y if a/px < b/py; any affordable bundle on the line if equal.

cards.f: Demand with perfect complements u = min(x, y)
cards.b: x = y = m/(px + py): the consumer buys at the kink.
The maximum utility attainable at prices p and income m; increasing in m and non-increasing in prices.
The change in demand from a change in relative prices, holding real income (purchasing power or utility) constant. For a price fall it never reduces demand.
The change in demand caused by the change in purchasing power that a price change brings, at the new relative prices.
A good whose demand rises when its price rises: it must be inferior, with an income effect that outweighs the substitution effect.

cards.f: Slutsky compensated income after px changes from p₀ to p₁
cards.b: m′ = m + x₀(p₁ − p₀): just enough to buy the original bundle at the new prices.
h(p, u): the bundle that minimises expenditure needed to reach utility u at prices p.
∂x/∂px = ∂h/∂px − x ∂x/∂m: total effect = substitution effect + income effect.
A curve showing how quantity demanded of a good changes with income, holding prices fixed.
The change in income needed after a price change to restore the consumer's original utility level.
MRTS = MPL/MPK: the rate at which labour can replace capital holding output constant; minus the slope of the isoquant.

cards.f: Returns to scale of Q = A K^α L^β
cards.b: Increasing if α + β > 1, constant if α + β = 1, decreasing if α + β < 1.
MRTS = w/r, equivalently MPL/w = MPK/r: the last pound spent on each input adds the same output.

cards.f: Where does MC cross AVC and ATC?
cards.b: At their minimum points: an average falls while the marginal is below it and rises while the marginal is above it.

cards.f: Diminishing marginal returns vs decreasing returns to scale
cards.b: Diminishing marginal returns: MP of one input falls as it alone rises. Decreasing returns to scale: scaling all inputs by t raises output by less than t.
A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered; it should not affect forward-looking decisions.
The lower envelope of the short-run average cost curves: the lowest unit cost when all inputs can be adjusted.
Short run: at least one input fixed. Long run: all inputs variable.

cards.f: Profit-maximising output for a price taker
cards.b: Produce where P = MC (on the rising part of MC), provided P ≥ minimum AVC.
Shut down if P < minimum AVC: revenue would not even cover avoidable (variable) costs.
Its marginal cost curve above the minimum of average variable cost.
P = MC = minimum LRAC, zero economic profit, and no incentive to enter or exit.

cards.f: First Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics (informal)
cards.b: Under conditions such as price-taking, complete markets and no externalities, a competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient.
An allocation where no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
Revenue just covers all costs including the opportunity cost of capital, so the firm earns a normal return.
MR = P(1 + 1/ε). MR > 0 only where demand is elastic (|ε| > 1).

cards.f: MR for linear inverse demand P = a − bQ
cards.b: MR = a − 2bQ: the same vertical intercept and twice the slope.
Produce where MR = MC and charge the price given by the demand curve at that output.
(P − MC)/P = −1/ε = 1/|ε| at the monopoly optimum: market power is greater when demand is less elastic.
Each buyer pays their maximum willingness to pay: output is efficient (no deadweight loss) but the firm takes all the surplus.
Set MR in each market equal to MC; the market with less elastic demand gets the higher price.

cards.f: Why a monopolist never produces on the inelastic part of demand
cards.b: There MR < 0, so cutting output would raise revenue and lower cost, increasing profit (with MC > 0).
An industry where one firm can supply the whole market at lower average cost than two or more firms, typically due to large fixed costs.
A strategy profile where each player's strategy is a best response to the others' strategies; no one gains by deviating alone.
A strategy that gives a strictly higher payoff than any other, whatever the other players do.

cards.f: Why is (Defect, Defect) the outcome of the prisoner's dilemma?
cards.b: Defect is strictly dominant for each player, so it is the unique Nash equilibrium, even though both would prefer mutual cooperation.

cards.f: Cournot best response with P = a − b(q₁ + q₂), cost c
cards.b: q₁ = (a − c − bq₂)/(2b); symmetric equilibrium q = (a − c)/(3b) for each firm.
Two firms selling identical goods with equal constant marginal cost and competing on price end up at P = MC, the competitive outcome.
The leader commits to a larger output, the follower responds with less, and the leader earns more than in Cournot.
Solving a sequential game from the last move backwards; it finds the subgame perfect equilibrium and removes non-credible threats.
Each player randomises so that the opponent is indifferent between the pure strategies the opponent uses.
MSC = MPC + MEC. The market produces where demand = MPC, more than the social optimum where demand = MSC.
A per-unit tax equal to the marginal external cost at the efficient output, so that private cost equals social cost (Pigou, 1920).
With well-defined property rights and low transaction costs, bargaining reaches the efficient outcome regardless of who holds the rights (Coase, 1960).
A good that is non-rival and non-excludable, e.g. national defence; markets under-provide it because of free riding.
Rival but non-excludable (e.g. fish stocks); prone to overuse, the tragedy of the commons.
Provide up to where the sum of individuals' marginal benefits (MRS) equals marginal cost.
Excludable but non-rival (at least until congestion), e.g. a subscription service.

cards.f: Advantage of tradable permits over uniform caps
cards.b: Total emissions are fixed, but firms trade so that abatement is done by those who can do it most cheaply.

questions.q: Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 3P − 20. What is the equilibrium?
questions.why: 100 − 2P = 3P − 20 gives 5P = 120, so P = 24, and Q = 100 − 48 = 52 (check: 72 − 20 = 52). P = 16, Q = 68 flips the sign of the supply intercept (solving 100 − 2P = 3P + 20); P = 20, Q = 60 drops the −20 intercept altogether (5P = 100); P = 24, Q = 72 finds the right price but reads quantity off 3P without subtracting 20. At each wrong price, or with the wrong quantity, quantity demanded and supplied are not equal.

questions.q: At the current price, demand for a good has elasticity −0.5. If the firm raises its price slightly, total revenue will
options: rise only if supply is elastic
questions.why: d(PQ)/dP = Q(1 + ε) = Q(0.5) > 0, so revenue rises: the percentage fall in quantity is smaller than the percentage rise in price. Revenue would fall only if |ε| > 1, would be unchanged only if |ε| = 1, and the supply elasticity is irrelevant to the seller's revenue along the demand curve.

questions.q: Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 3P − 20. A per-unit tax of 5 is imposed on sellers. Find the price paid by buyers, the price received by sellers, the quantity traded, the tax revenue and the deadweight loss.
markScheme: New supply in terms of buyer price: Qs = 3(Pb − 5) − 20 = 3Pb − 35
Pb = 27 and Ps = 22
Revenue = 5 × 46 = 230
questions.modelAnswer: Without the tax, 100 − 2P = 3P − 20 gives P = 24 and Q = 52. With the tax, sellers keep Ps = Pb − 5, so supply is 3(Pb − 5) − 20 = 3Pb − 35. Setting 100 − 2Pb = 3Pb − 35 gives Pb = 27, so Ps = 22 and Q = 100 − 54 = 46. Buyers pay 3 more and sellers receive 2 less, so buyers bear 60% of the tax because demand is less price-responsive than supply. Revenue = 5 × 46 = 230. The deadweight loss is the triangle ½ × 5 × (52 − 46) = 15.

questions.q: For x, y > 0, which function does NOT represent the same preferences as u = xy?
questions.why: ln x + ln y = ln(xy), (xy)² and xy + 10 are all strictly increasing transformations of xy when xy > 0, so they rank bundles identically. −xy reverses the ranking, so it represents the opposite preferences.

questions.q: For u = xy², what is the MRS (MUx/MUy) at the bundle (4, 2)?
questions.why: MUx = y² = 4 and MUy = 2xy = 16, so MRS = 4/16 = 0.25 (the formula is y/(2x)). 0.5 forgets the factor 2 from the exponent (taking MUy = xy = 8); 4 inverts the ratio (MUy/MUx = 16/4); 1 evaluates y/(2x) with x and y swapped, i.e. at (2, 4).

questions.q: For u(x, y) = x^a y^(1−a) with 0 < a < 1, derive the MRS. Show that v = a ln x + (1 − a) ln y gives the same MRS, and explain why.
markScheme: MUx = a x^(a−1) y^(1−a), MUy = (1 − a) x^a y^(−a)
For v: ∂v/∂x = a/x, ∂v/∂y = (1 − a)/y, ratio also [a/(1 − a)](y/x)
Reason: v = ln u is a strictly increasing transformation, so it represents the same preferences (utility is ordinal)
questions.modelAnswer: MUx = a x^(a−1) y^(1−a) and MUy = (1 − a) x^a y^(−a). Dividing, MRS = [a/(1 − a)] × x^(a−1−a) y^(1−a+a) = [a/(1 − a)](y/x). For v, ∂v/∂x = a/x and ∂v/∂y = (1 − a)/y, so the ratio is [a/(1 − a)](y/x), the same. This is because v = ln u, a strictly increasing transformation; it changes the size of marginal utilities but not their ratio, so the indifference curves and every choice are unchanged. Utility is ordinal.

questions.q: u = x^½ y^½, income m = 100, prices px = 2 and py = 5. What is the optimal bundle?
questions.why: Cobb–Douglas with a = ½ means half of income goes on each good: x = 50/2 = 25, y = 50/5 = 10. (20, 12) is affordable but does not satisfy MRS = y/x = px/py = 0.4; (50, 20) costs 200; (10, 25) swaps the goods and costs 145.

questions.q: A consumer has u = x + 2y, income 40, px = 3 and py = 4. What do they buy?
options: Any bundle on the budget line
questions.why: Marginal utility per pound is 1/3 for x and 2/4 = 0.5 for y, so all income goes on y: 40/4 = 10. Buying only x gives utility 13.3 < 20; (5, 5) costs 35 and is not optimal; indifference between bundles requires a/px = b/py, which fails here.

questions.q: Using the Lagrangian method, find the utility-maximising bundle for u = x^(1/3) y^(2/3) when m = 90, px = 3 and py = 6. Verify that MRS = px/py at your answer.
markScheme: Sets up L = x^(1/3) y^(2/3) + λ(90 − 3x − 6y) (or uses logs)
FOCs give MRS = y/(2x) = px/py = ½, so y = x
Substitutes into the budget: 3x + 6x = 90
Verifies MRS = 10/20 = ½ = 3/6 and spending 30 + 60 = 90
questions.modelAnswer: Maximise ln u = (1/3)ln x + (2/3)ln y subject to 3x + 6y = 90. L = (1/3)ln x + (2/3)ln y + λ(90 − 3x − 6y). FOCs: 1/(3x) = 3λ and 2/(3y) = 6λ. Dividing, (1/(3x))/(2/(3y)) = 3/6, so y/(2x) = ½ and y = x. Then 3x + 6x = 90 gives x* = 10 and y* = 10. This matches the Cobb–Douglas formulae x = (1/3)(90)/3 and y = (2/3)(90)/6. Check: MRS = y/(2x) = 0.5 = px/py, and spending is 30 + 60 = 90.

questions.q: For a Giffen good, which statement is correct?
options: It is a normal good with a large income effect
It is an inferior good whose income effect outweighs the substitution effect
Any inferior good is a Giffen good
questions.why: A Giffen good's demand moves in the same direction as its price, which needs a perverse income effect (inferior good) large enough to beat the substitution effect. For a normal good the income effect reinforces the substitution effect; the substitution effect is never positive; and most inferior goods are not Giffen, because the income effect is usually smaller.

questions.q: With u = xy, m = 120 and py = 1, px falls from 3 to 2. Using Slutsky compensation, what is the substitution effect on x?
questions.why: x = m/(2px). Original x = 20; compensated income = 120 − 20 = 100, giving x = 100/4 = 25, so the substitution effect is +5 (and the income effect 30 − 25 = +5). +10 is the total effect; +4.49 is the Hicksian substitution effect; and a price fall cannot give a negative substitution effect.

questions.q: Explain, using income and substitution effects, why the demand curve for a normal good must slope downwards, but the demand curve for an inferior good might not.
markScheme: Substitution effect of a price fall never lowers quantity demanded (with smooth, strictly convex preferences it raises it)
A price fall raises real income
Normal good: income effect also raises quantity, so both effects push the same way and demand slopes down
Inferior good: income effect reduces quantity; if larger than the substitution effect, demand slopes up (Giffen)
questions.modelAnswer: When the price of a good falls, the substitution effect (holding real income constant) never lowers the quantity demanded, and with smooth convex indifference curves it raises it, because the good is now relatively cheaper. The price fall also raises the consumer's real income. For a normal good, higher real income raises demand, so the income effect works in the same direction and the quantity demanded definitely rises: demand slopes down. For an inferior good, higher real income reduces demand, so the income effect works against the substitution effect. Usually it is smaller, so demand still slopes down; but if it is larger, quantity falls when price falls and the good is a Giffen good with an upward-sloping demand curve.

questions.q: The production function Q = K^0.3 L^0.5 exhibits
questions.why: 0.3 + 0.5 = 0.8 < 1, so doubling both inputs raises output by a factor of 2^0.8 ≈ 1.74 < 2: decreasing returns to scale. The marginal product of labour is 0.5 K^0.3 L^−0.5, which falls as L rises, so it is diminishing, not increasing.

questions.q: A firm's marginal cost is below its average total cost at the current output. If it produces one more unit, average total cost will
questions.why: When the cost of the extra unit is below the current average, adding it pulls the average down. ATC rises only when MC is above it, and is flat (at its minimum) where MC = ATC.

questions.q: A firm has Q = K^½ L^½, wage w = 4 and rental rate r = 1. (a) Find the long-run cost function. (b) With capital fixed at K = 16, find the short-run total cost and the output at which short-run average cost is lowest. Comment.
markScheme: Cost minimisation: MPL/MPK = K/L = w/r = 4, so K = 4L
L = Q/2, K = 2Q, so C(Q) = 4Q (LRAC = LRMC = 4)
Short run: Q = 4√L so L = Q²/16; STC = 16 + Q²/4
SAC = 16/Q + Q/4, minimised at Q = 8 (where SAC = SMC = 4)
Comment: at Q = 8, K = 16 is the long-run optimal choice, so SAC touches LRAC there
questions.modelAnswer: (a) MPL = ½K^½L^−½ and MPK = ½K^−½L^½, so MRTS = K/L. Setting K/L = w/r = 4 gives K = 4L. Then Q = √(4L·L) = 2L, so L = Q/2 and K = 2Q. Cost = 4(Q/2) + 1(2Q) = 4Q, so long-run average and marginal cost are both 4 (constant returns to scale). (b) With K = 16, Q = 4√L, so L = Q²/16. STC = rK + wL = 16 + 4Q²/16 = 16 + Q²/4. SAC = 16/Q + Q/4 and SMC = Q/2. SAC is lowest where SMC = SAC: Q/2 = 16/Q + Q/4, so Q²/4 = 16 and Q = 8, giving SAC = 2 + 2 = 4. This equals LRAC, because K = 16 is exactly the cost-minimising capital for Q = 8 (K = 2Q): the short-run curve touches the long-run curve there.

questions.q: A competitive firm faces a price above its minimum average variable cost but below its minimum average total cost. In the short run it should
options: produce where P = MC and accept a loss
raise its price to cover average total cost
questions.why: Revenue covers all variable costs and part of the fixed costs, so producing where P = MC loses less than shutting down (which loses all fixed costs). A price taker cannot raise its price; and the profit-maximising output is where P = MC, not where AVC is lowest.

questions.q: Identical firms each have C(q) = 100 + q² and market demand is Q = 1000 − 10P. In long-run equilibrium, how many firms are there?
questions.why: Minimum AC is where 100/q = q, so q = 10 and AC = 20. The long-run price is 20, market demand is 1000 − 200 = 800, and 800/10 = 80 firms. 800 is market output, not the number of firms; 100 divides the demand intercept 1000 by q = 10, as if the price were zero; 50 divides 1000 by the price 20 instead of first finding the quantity demanded.

questions.q: Each identical firm in a competitive industry has C(q) = 100 + q², and market demand is Q = 1000 − 10P. Find the long-run equilibrium price, output per firm and number of firms. Explain why economic profit is zero.
markScheme: MC = 2q, AC = 100/q + q
Minimum AC at q = 10 (where MC = AC), AC = 20
Long-run price P = 20
Market Q = 800, so n = 80 firms
Zero profit because entry/exit drives price to minimum AC (any profit attracts entry)
questions.modelAnswer: MC = 2q and AC = 100/q + q. AC is minimised where MC = AC: 2q = 100/q + q, so q² = 100 and q = 10, giving minimum AC = 10 + 10 = 20. In the long run free entry and exit push the price to minimum average cost, so P = 20 and each firm produces 10 (where P = MC = 20). Market demand at P = 20 is 1000 − 200 = 800, so there are 800/10 = 80 firms. Each earns revenue 200 and has cost 100 + 100 = 200, so economic profit is zero. If price were above 20, positive profit would attract entry and push price down; if below, losses would cause exit.

questions.q: At a monopolist's profit-maximising output, the price elasticity of demand is −4. What is the Lerner index (P − MC)/P?
questions.why: The mark-up rule gives (P − MC)/P = −1/ε = 1/4 = 0.25. 0.75 is 1 − 1/4 (the ratio MC/P); 4 is |ε| itself; and the Lerner index is non-negative because P ≥ MC.

questions.q: A firm practises third-degree price discrimination between students and other customers with the same constant marginal cost. If students' demand is more elastic, then
options: both groups pay the same price
students pay a price equal to marginal cost
questions.why: Setting MR = MC in each market and using the mark-up rule (P − MC)/P = 1/|ε|, the group with more elastic demand gets a smaller mark-up, i.e. a lower price. Equal prices would mean no discrimination, and the price for students is still above MC unless their demand is perfectly elastic.

questions.q: A monopolist faces P = 100 − 2Q and has constant marginal cost 20. Find its output, price and profit, the deadweight loss compared with perfect competition, and verify the Lerner index.
markScheme: MR = MC gives Q = 20, P = 60, profit 800
Competitive outcome: P = 20, Q = 40
questions.modelAnswer: Revenue is (100 − 2Q)Q, so MR = 100 − 4Q. Setting MR = 20 gives Q = 20, and the demand curve gives P = 100 − 40 = 60. Profit = (60 − 20) × 20 = 800 (no fixed costs). Under perfect competition P = MC = 20, so 100 − 2Q = 20 and Q = 40. The deadweight loss is the triangle between demand and MC from Q = 20 to Q = 40: ½ × (60 − 20) × (40 − 20) = 400. At Q = 20, demand is Q = 50 − P/2, so dQ/dP = −½ and ε = −½ × 60/20 = −1.5. The Lerner index is (60 − 20)/60 = 2/3 = 1/|ε|, as the mark-up rule predicts.

questions.q: Two Cournot duopolists face P = 100 − Q and each has constant marginal cost 10. What is each firm's equilibrium output?
questions.why: q = (a − c)/(3b) = 90/3 = 30 each, so total output is 60 and P = 40. 45 is the monopoly output; 22.5 is half the monopoly output (the collusive split); 15 wrongly treats (a − c)/(3b) = 30 as total industry output and halves it.

questions.q: Two firms sell an identical product, have the same constant marginal cost and compete by simultaneously setting prices. In equilibrium the price is
options: between marginal cost and the monopoly price
questions.why: In the Bertrand model any price above MC can be undercut by the rival, who then takes the whole market, so the only equilibrium is P = MC. The monopoly price and intermediate prices are undercut; pricing below MC would mean losses, so it is not a best response.

questions.q: Find all Nash equilibria (pure and mixed) of this game. Payoffs are (row, column): (U, L) = (4, 3); (U, R) = (1, 1); (D, L) = (2, 0); (D, R) = (3, 2).
markScheme: Best responses: row plays U against L (4 > 2) and D against R (3 > 1)
Column plays L against U (3 > 1) and R against D (2 > 0)
Pure equilibria: (U, L) and (D, R)
Mixed: row plays U with p where 3p = p + 2(1 − p), so p = ½
Column plays L with q where 4q + (1 − q) = 2q + 3(1 − q), so q = ½
questions.modelAnswer: Row's best response to L is U (4 > 2) and to R is D (3 > 1). Column's best response to U is L (3 > 1) and to D is R (2 > 0). So (U, L) and (D, R) are pure-strategy Nash equilibria; (U, R) and (D, L) are not. For the mixed equilibrium, let row play U with probability p. Column's payoff from L is 3p and from R is p + 2(1 − p) = 2 − p; indifference gives 3p = 2 − p, so p = ½. Let column play L with probability q. Row's payoff from U is 4q + (1 − q) = 1 + 3q and from D is 2q + 3(1 − q) = 3 − q; indifference gives q = ½. So there is also a mixed equilibrium with each player choosing each strategy with probability ½ (expected payoffs 2.5 for row and 1.5 for column).

questions.q: A good is non-excludable but rival. It is best described as
questions.why: Rival and non-excludable goods are common resources (such as ocean fish stocks), which tend to be overused. Public goods are non-rival as well as non-excludable; club goods are excludable and non-rival; private goods are rival and excludable.

questions.q: According to the Coase theorem, if a factory and a neighbouring laundry can bargain at zero cost over the factory's smoke, then
options: the efficient level of smoke is reached only if the laundry has the legal right to clean air
the efficient level of smoke is reached whichever party has the legal right
the government must impose a Pigouvian tax for efficiency
smoke will always be reduced to zero
questions.why: Coase's point is that with well-defined rights and costless bargaining, the parties will trade to the efficient outcome regardless of who holds the right; the allocation affects who pays whom. No tax is needed under these assumptions, and the efficient level of smoke is generally not zero.

questions.q: Demand for a good is P = 100 − Q, private marginal cost is MPC = 20 + Q, and production causes external damage of 10 per unit. Find the market output, the socially efficient output, the deadweight loss and the Pigouvian tax that corrects the market.
markScheme: Market: 100 − Q = 20 + Q, so Q = 40 (P = 60)
MSC = 30 + Q; optimum 100 − Q = 30 + Q, so Q = 35 (P = 65)
Pigouvian tax = 10 per unit (MEC at the optimum)
Explains that the tax makes firms face the full social cost
questions.modelAnswer: The market ignores the external cost, so it sets 100 − Q = 20 + Q, giving Q = 40 and P = 60. Social marginal cost is MSC = 20 + Q + 10 = 30 + Q, so the efficient output solves 100 − Q = 30 + Q, giving Q = 35 and P = 65. For units 35 to 40, MSC exceeds marginal benefit; the gap rises from 0 to 10, so the deadweight loss is ½ × 10 × (40 − 35) = 25. A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost at the optimum, 10 per unit, raises the firms' private cost to 30 + Q, so the market chooses Q = 35 and the deadweight loss disappears.

questions.q:
A consumer has utility u(x, y) = xy and income m = 120. The price of y is 1. The price of x falls from 3 to 2.
(a) Use the Lagrangian method to derive the Marshallian demand functions for x and y. [6]
(b) Find the consumer's optimal bundle before and after the price change. [3]
(c) Decompose the change in demand for x into substitution and income effects using Slutsky compensation. [6]
(d) Repeat the decomposition using Hicks compensation, and explain why the answers differ. [6]
(e) Calculate the compensating variation of the price fall and interpret it. [4]
markScheme: (a) L = xy + λ(m − px x − py y); FOCs y = λpx, x = λpy; so px x = py y and x = m/(2px), y = m/(2py)
(c) Slutsky income m′ = 120 + 20(2 − 3) = 100; compensated x = 25; SE = +5, IE = +5
(d) Original utility 1200; Hicksian demand at px = 2, py = 1 solves y = 2x, xy = 1200: x = √600 ≈ 24.49; SE ≈ +4.49, IE ≈ +5.51

(d) Difference: Slutsky keeps the old bundle affordable, which lets the consumer reach a higher indifference curve; Hicks holds utility fixed; they approximately coincide for small price changes (exactly in the limit)
(e) Expenditure function e = 2√(px py u); e(2, 1, 1200) = 2√2400 ≈ 97.98
(e) CV ≈ 120 − 97.98 ≈ 22.02: the income that could be taken away after the price fall to leave the consumer as well off as before
Clear statement that x is a normal good here (income effect positive) and good use of a diagram
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Maximise xy subject to px x + py y = m. L = xy + λ(m − px x − py y). FOCs: ∂L/∂x = y − λpx = 0, ∂L/∂y = x − λpy = 0, and the budget constraint. Dividing the first two, y/x = px/py, so py y = px x: spending is split equally. Substituting into the budget, 2px x = m, so x = m/(2px) and y = m/(2py).

(b) Before: x = 120/6 = 20 and y = 120/2 = 60. After: x = 120/4 = 30 and y = 60 (spending on y is unchanged at half of income). The total effect on x is +10.

(c) Slutsky compensation keeps the original bundle just affordable: m′ = m + x₀(p₁ − p₀) = 120 + 20(2 − 3) = 100. At px = 2 with income 100, x = 100/4 = 25. Substitution effect = 25 − 20 = +5. Income effect = 30 − 25 = +5. Both are positive for a price fall, so x is a normal good.

(d) Hicks compensation keeps utility at its original level u₀ = 20 × 60 = 1200. Minimise 2x + y subject to xy = 1200. Tangency gives y/x = px/py = 2, so y = 2x and 2x² = 1200, so x = √600 ≈ 24.49 (y ≈ 48.99). Substitution effect ≈ 24.49 − 20 = +4.49, and income effect ≈ 30 − 24.49 = +5.51. The decompositions differ because Slutsky compensation lets the consumer buy the old bundle, and since relative prices have changed they can then do strictly better than u₀ by substituting, so Slutsky compensation is slightly generous. Hicks compensation holds utility exactly constant. For an infinitesimal price change the two coincide.

(e) The expenditure function for u = xy is e(px, py, u) = 2√(px py u) (from px x = py y = √(px py u) at the cost-minimising bundle). Compensating variation = m − e(new prices, u₀) = 120 − 2√(2 × 1 × 1200) = 120 − 2√2400 ≈ 120 − 97.98 = 22.02. Interpretation: after the price fall the consumer could give up about 22.02 of income and still be exactly as well off as before. It is a money measure of the gain from the price cut. (Check: with income 97.98 at the new prices, demands are x ≈ 24.49 and y ≈ 48.99, and xy ≈ 1200.)

questions.q:
Two firms produce an identical good. Inverse market demand is P = 120 − Q, where Q = q₁ + q₂, and each firm has constant marginal cost 30 and no fixed costs.
(a) Derive each firm's best-response function in the Cournot model and find the Cournot–Nash equilibrium quantities, price and profits. [7]
(b) If the firms collude to maximise joint profit and split output equally, find each firm's profit. Show that each firm has an incentive to deviate, and relate this to the prisoner's dilemma. [6]
(c) Now suppose firm 1 chooses its quantity first and firm 2 observes it (Stackelberg). Find the equilibrium quantities, price and profits. [6]
(d) What would happen if the firms competed in prices instead (Bertrand)? Rank the market structures by total surplus and calculate the deadweight loss under Cournot. [6]
markScheme: (a) π₁ = (120 − q₁ − q₂ − 30)q₁; FOC 90 − 2q₁ − q₂ = 0; BR q₁ = (90 − q₂)/2 (symmetric for firm 2)
(a) Equilibrium q₁ = q₂ = 30, Q = 60, P = 60, profit 900 each
(b) Monopoly Q = 45, P = 75, joint profit 2025, so 1012.5 each
(b) Best response to 22.5 is 33.75; P = 63.75; deviator earns about 1139 > 1012.5; collusion is not a Nash equilibrium (prisoner's dilemma)
(c) Leader maximises (90 − q₁ − (90 − q₁)/2)q₁ = ((90 − q₁)/2)q₁, giving q₁ = 45, q₂ = 22.5, P = 52.5, profits 1012.5 and 506.25
(d) Bertrand: P = MC = 30, Q = 90, zero profits, total surplus 4050
(d) Ranking by total surplus: Bertrand/competition (4050) > Stackelberg (3796.875) > Cournot (3600) > collusion/monopoly (3037.5)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Firm 1's profit is π₁ = (120 − q₁ − q₂)q₁ − 30q₁ = (90 − q₁ − q₂)q₁. FOC: 90 − 2q₁ − q₂ = 0, so the best response is q₁ = (90 − q₂)/2; by symmetry q₂ = (90 − q₁)/2. In a symmetric equilibrium q = (90 − q)/2, so q = 30 for each firm. Total output is 60, price is 120 − 60 = 60, and each firm earns (60 − 30) × 30 = 900.

(b) Joint profit (90 − Q)Q is maximised at Q = 45, with P = 75 and total profit 45 × 45 = 2025, so each firm earns 1012.5 by producing 22.5. But firm 1's best response to q₂ = 22.5 is q₁ = (90 − 22.5)/2 = 33.75. Then Q = 56.25, P = 63.75, and firm 1 earns (63.75 − 30) × 33.75 ≈ 1139.06 > 1012.5, while firm 2's profit falls to 33.75 × 22.5 ≈ 759.38. So the collusive output is not a Nash equilibrium. Each firm has a private incentive to expand, and if both do so they end up at the Cournot outcome with 900 each, worse than collusion: the structure of a prisoner's dilemma. Collusion can be sustained only with enforcement or repeated interaction (and is illegal under competition law).

(c) Firm 1 anticipates q₂ = (90 − q₁)/2. Its profit is (90 − q₁ − (90 − q₁)/2)q₁ = ((90 − q₁)/2)q₁. Maximising: (90 − 2q₁)/2 = 0, so q₁ = 45. Then q₂ = (90 − 45)/2 = 22.5, Q = 67.5 and P = 52.5. Profits: firm 1 earns (52.5 − 30) × 45 = 1012.5 and firm 2 earns 22.5 × 22.5 = 506.25. The leader gains from commitment (1012.5 > 900) and the follower loses (506.25 < 900).

(d) With price competition and identical products, any price above 30 can be profitably undercut, so the Bertrand equilibrium is P = MC = 30, Q = 90, and both firms make zero profit. Total surplus (CS + profits) in each case: Bertrand: CS = ½ × 90 × 90 = 4050, profit 0, total 4050 (the efficient level). Stackelberg: CS = ½ × 67.5² = 2278.125, profits 1518.75, total 3796.875. Cournot: CS = ½ × 60 × 60 = 1800, profits 1800, total 3600. Collusion (monopoly): CS = ½ × 45 × 45 = 1012.5, profit 2025, total 3037.5. So total surplus ranks Bertrand > Stackelberg > Cournot > collusion. The Cournot deadweight loss is 4050 − 3600 = 450, which equals the triangle ½ × (60 − 30) × (90 − 60) = 450.
